```json
{"body":"Three separate problems are tangled together here, and it helps to treat them separately: what "done" means for each chore, who is responsible given current schedules, and the friend who has stopped talking.

The recurring "we agreed but later disagreed about what it meant" pattern is usually not a memory problem or a bad-faith problem. Verbal chore agreements leave almost everything unspecified — how clean is clean, by when, what happens when circumstances change — and each person later fills in the gaps with whatever reading suits them, so both sides can honestly believe the other broke the deal. The fix is to make agreements specific and keep a shared record: a note on the fridge, a whiteboard, a pinned message in a group chat. Before assigning a task, agree what done looks like (kitchen done includes wiping the counters, or doesn't) and a timeframe — "by Sunday night," not "soon." This isn't about distrust; it removes the gap where reinterpretation lives.

Changing schedules mean any split is provisional. Build in renegotiation so that adjusting an agreement is normal rather than a sign of failure: a short standing check-in, or a rule that when someone's schedule changes they flag it and the split gets revisited. A useful default is that silence leaves the old agreement in force, so nobody quietly drifts out of a commitment. Framing it as "the agreement expired, let's renew" keeps it from becoming "you broke your promise."

The avoiding friend is the delicate part. Avoidance is information: they may feel blamed, outvoted, or convinced the talks produce nothing durable, and pressing harder for the same conversation will deepen the retreat. Before raising chores with them again, ask a smaller question — what makes these talks unpleasant, and what format would they actually take part in: a ten-minute slot, one item at a time in the chat, talking while cooking together. Repair the channel before pushing content through it. If they won't meet, you can still propose a written split and invite objections by a date, treating no reply as agreement with an early review attached — but converting silence into consent can feel unfair, so hold that move loosely.

Two caveats. Keep criticism about tasks, not people, and raise misses promptly and specifically rather than storing them up. And if one person refuses every format, no chore system will fix that: the real problem is then the living arrangement itself, and the honest options are a mediated conversation, shrinking what you share, or reconsidering things at renewal.","commitments":"The account rests on one empirical claim worth checking before anything else: that the disputes track vagueness and change rather than reliability or bad faith. If the reader finds that written, specific agreements are still being broken, the diagnosis is wrong and the process advice will not help, and the problem lies elsewhere.

Taking up the written-agreement proposal commits the reader to specifying what "done" means for each contested chore before assigning it, which requires conceding that standards legitimately differ between the three of them and must actually be negotiated rather than treated as obvious. It also depends on everyone consulting the same record, so a chat or board the avoiding friend never reads fails silently.

The check-in proposal presumes schedules will keep changing, as the reader reports; its value drops if the household stabilizes, and it presumes at least the avoiding friend will accept some meeting format, which is exactly what is in doubt. The default rule that silence leaves the old agreement in force is contestable from the other side as well — it can entrench an arrangement one person never wanted.

The proposal to treat non-response to a written offer as consent is the most vulnerable item: it risks converting withdrawal into agreement and deepening the friend's retreat. Anyone adopting it should expect the fairness objection and be ready to attach an early review date or drop the move entirely.

A criticism the whole approach invites: even the light version imposes ongoing initiation and upkeep on the reader, unpaid coordination labor falling on the person least at fault. That cost is real and may not be sustainable, and nothing here distributes it.

The account assumes the reader's own agreements are not a major source of the vagueness; using it fairly includes auditing one's own habits first.

Finally, an unresolved problem the account does not solve: if the avoiding friend rejects every format, no chore-level mechanism applies and only escalation paths remain — mediated conversation, reduced shared space, or non-renewal. Whether any of those is acceptable is left to the reader."}
```

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?
